utterances.text: Chamber will now deliver its decision on the Gotovina Defence's and the Prosecution's request for admission of evidence -- for admission of evidence of Milan Babic, pursuant to Rule 92 quater. On 15th of May, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion requesting admission of parts of Milan Babic's plea agreement and transcript of his trial testimony in prior cases before the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 92 quater. On the 28th of May, 2009, the Prosecution filed a response, not objecting to the motion. At the same time, the Prosecution requested admission of further transcripts of trial testimony of this witness, pursuant to Rule 92 quater. Rule 92 quater provides that written statements or transcripts of unavailable persons may be admitted, whether or not the written statement is in the form prescribed by Rule 92 bis, if the Chamber is satisfied of the person's unavailability and finds from the circumstances in which the statement was made and recorded that it is reliable. Rule 92 quater further provides that, if the evidence goes to proof of acts and conduct of an accused as charged in the indictment, this may be a factor against the admission of such evidence. In addition, the Chamber must also be satisfied that the evidence meets the general requirements of admissibility under Rule 89(C); namely, that it is relevant and has probative value. Considering submission by the Gotovina Defence that Milan Babic is deceased and a report attached to the motion detailing the circumstances of his death, the Chamber is satisfied that Milan Babic is unavailable, pursuant to Rule 92 quater. In order to rely on an evidentiary basis that is as broad as possible, the Chamber will consider the material tendered by the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution together. The transcript excerpts offered into evidence by the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution contain testimony of Milan Babic given in other cases before the Tribunal. They were made under oath and were subject to cross-examination in these proceedings. The Chamber is mindful of the fact that the parts of the plea agreement which the Gotovina Defence seeks to have admitted came into existence through an agreement of the parties in the Milan Babic case. However, the Chamber also considers that the Chamber in that case established that a sufficient factual basis for the plea agreement existed. Moreover neither the Prosecution, nor the Cermak or Markac Defence have expressed any concerns with regard to the reliability of the relevant parts of the plea agreement. Furthermore, the Chamber has received ample evidence that corroborates the main issues touched upon in the transcripts and the plea agreement excerpt, such as Witness Galbraith's testimony on the negotiations of the Z-4 plan. The Chamber therefore finds that these documents are reliable for the purposes of Rule 92 quater. The main topics of the transcripts and the plea agreement excerpt are Serbia's involvement in the establishment and the functioning of the institutions of the RSK through imposing decisions or providing assistance in form of financing, supplying arms, or employing the JNA. This evidence relates to the question of the nature of the armed conflict that is at issue in the Gotovina et al case and is therefore relevant. The documents further describe the diplomatic negotiations prior to Operation Storm, in particular, concerning the Z-4 plan, which constitutes relevant background to the issues of this case. Evidence on propagandistic Serb media reports instilling fears in the Serb population in the Krajina of the Croatian government, as well as evidence on Serb refugees after Operation Storm, also has relevance to this case. In light of the nature of the tendered material, the Chamber will simply disregard individual pages for which no relevance can be established, rather than singling them out for non-admission. Since reliability is a component part of the probative value of a piece of evidence, there is no need to re-examine the probative value of the documents at issue, as their reliability has already been established within the context of Rule 92 quater. Consequently, the Chamber finds that the transcripts and the parts of the plea agreement of Milan Babic as tendered by the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution respectively meet the requirements of Rule 92 quater and Rule 89(C). The Chamber therefore admits them into evidence under seal. The Chamber instructs the registrar to assign exhibit numbers to the admitted documents and to inform the parties and the Chamber of the exhibit numbers so assigned. For the benefit of the transparency of the trial, the Chamber invites the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution to review whether a request to rescind the protective measures pursuant to Rule 75(G) is apposite, and inform the Chamber of their respective positions within two weeks. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter.

On the 22nd of July of this year, the Gotovina Defence filed a written motion seeking the admission of 11 statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The statements were attached to the motion as Annex A. These statements had already been tendered on the 16th of May, 2008, during the cross-examination of Witness Vladimir Gojanovic. On the 11 of June, 2008, however, the Chamber denied the admission of these statements because the procedural requirements for admission were not fulfilled at that time. On that occasion, the Chamber noted that this did not mean that these statements could not be admitted at a later stage with the required attestations. This can be found at transcript page 4.819. On the 29th of July, 2009, the Prosecution filed a response to the Gotovina Defence motion of the 22nd of July stating that it did not object to the admission of the 11 written statements if it could cross-examine four of the witnesses whose statements were being tendered. On the 25th of August, 2009, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the four witnesses and decided that those witnesses should be heard via video-conference link. A written decision for the 25th of August, 2009 decision allowing for cross-examination of those witnesses will follow. The four witnesses testified on the 9th of September, 2009, and their statements were admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter on that day. These admissions can be found on transcript pages 21.342, 21.363, 21.390, and 21.409. In the present decision, the Chamber will detail with the remaining seven statements attached to the Gotovina Defence's motion. Pursuant to 92 bis (A), a chamber may admit, in whole or in part, the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the Indictment. Some factors in favour of admitting evidence in the form of a written statement include that it is of a cumulative nature and that it relates to relevant historical, political, or military background. Factors against admission include, but are not limited to, whether there is an overriding public interest in the evidence in question being presented orally and whether a party can demonstrate that the nature and source of the written statement renders it unreliable. Additionally, the statements must follow the form required in Rule 92 bis (B) and be relevant and probative, pursuant to Rule 89(C). The Chamber notes initially that the seven statements do not concern the acts or conduct of the accused. The Chamber considers that the information contained in the statements is of a cumulative nature and concerns similar facts provided in the oral testimony of the four witnesses who were cross-examined on the 9th of September, 2009. The parties were given ample opportunity to examine these four witnesses as well as Witness Gojanovic on the information contained in the seven statements. Therefore, the Chamber decides to admit the seven statements, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. While these seven statements meet the requirements for admission, the Chamber will only determine the weight to be attached to them, if any, in the context of the evidence before it as a whole, and more specifically, the testimony of Vladimir Gojanovic and of the four witnesses that were cross-examined on the 9th of September, 2009. In its response of the 29th of July, 2009, the Prosecution stated that it would address the probative value of all 11 statements in its closing submissions. The Chamber invites the Gotovina Defence to make similar submissions. The Gotovina Defence informally told the Chamber that no protective measures are sought for these seven witnesses. The Registrar has informally told the Chamber that the attestations for each of the seven 92 bis statements will be added to the exhibit number previously assigned to each statement on the 16th of May, 2008 as follows: The statement of Ratko Despot, given on the 18th of May, 2008, was assigned Exhibit D206.

On the 10th of September, 2009, the Prosecution filed its response indicating that it did not object to the request, and the Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence did not respond. As the Chamber has held in previous decisions, the party seeking protective measures must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that a witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can, for example, be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. Witness IC-2 is a Croatian Serb currently residing in Croatia. The witness has indicated that his testimony could cause hostile reactions in the Serb community of his hometown. He has expressed his concerns for himself and his family. The witness is expected to testify about how the Croatian authorities treated him after Operation Storm, as well as about an event, which may identify him to the Serb community of his hometown. Earlier this year, the witness received frequent threats over the phone, as well as from neighbours and others in his immediate surroundings. Recently, a person closely related to the events the witness is expected to testify about, insulted and threatened the witness, making reference to his pending testimony in The Hague. Around the same time, one of the witness's neighbours damaged some of the witness's property. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that the Cermak Defence has demonstrated an objectively grounded risk as to the security and welfare of Witness IC-2, should it become known that he has given evidence before this Tribunal. The Chamber considers that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of the witness, the only effective way to protect his identity is to hear his testimony in closed session. The Chamber grants the motion for the trial-related protective measures of testimony in closed session and pseudonym. utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, General Feldi, to a video, and these are excerpts, Mr. President, from P2532. This is OTP's interview with General Cermak in 2004. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Brian Foster: Going back to, then, the special nature of your position, you weren't -- you say, you tell me, formally attached to Gotovina and Cervenko. You had a different route in terms of perhaps somebody you needed to go to if there were things you wanted to discuss. Could you explain what that route was in sense of your subordination, who did you report to? Who did you discuss problems with, other than the ones you mentioned with Gotovina? Ivan Cermak: First of all, all these jobs that I was dealing with nobody was interested, as far as the military was concerned. Because Cervenko was certainly not concerned about the fact that I was dealing with soup kitchens and cleaning up the town and issues relating to the town itself. I was more connected with the office of the president. Because I went down there with special tasks from him. And I was often in touch with Sarinic, and Vesna Skare Ozbolt, and the president on several occasions. Brian Foster: Okay. And while we're perhaps talking about the relationship with the president, did you -- did you put anything in writing to the president or to the president's office about any problems that you were having down there? Ivan Cermak: I didn't put anything in writing to the president because it was not necessary. And I advised him -- discussing things with him. I asked him to do certain things, to reinforce the police. He said he knew. And that things would be done to stop this. Don't forget that the president was certainly better informed in Zagreb than I was. Because he got all the reports from the police ... from the police, from the security services, from SIS, from SZUP and also meetings -- Cedo Prodanovic: And international organisations ... Ivan Cermak: ... also pointed out to him. Because all letters and everything that the international community was telling me also automatically went for coordination to the office in Zadar, from the coordination office in Zadar to the Ministry of Defence in Zagreb. And, as far as I know, also to the centre for the international community in Zagreb, which is clearly stated in your papers as well. That they sent -- it clearly says that they sent all these warnings of what was going on and that the Croatian government never responded. There were institutions of the government, all the way to the government, institutions of the state that were responsible to prevent all this that happened and they were well-informed. Brian Foster: So, you were saying that you -- you had verbal communication with President Tudjman and you advised him on -- I don't know how many occasions -- of these problems, and he, you're saying, responded that he would deal with them and that he knew about it. Is that what you're saying? Ivan Cermak: [Indiscernible] ... send them reports of what I was doing, conversation, electricity, we have the hospital ... over the hospital, I couldn't -- this is writing to the president. But those are my tasks, and this was my private initiative that I took. Brian Foster: Okay. So, yes. Ivan Cermak: [No interpretation] Brian Foster: It's just that, your position there, and this is where we struggle always, you've said that you were not a classical garrison commander, therefore, you didn't come under that normal command route from the Main Staff. But I'm still not quite clear as to who you did come under, other than the president himself. Jadranka Slokovic: Also president. Ivan Cermak: I said this all before. And I said that at the beginning already, and I say it again, that had I been in this command structure, I would have gotten my orders from General Gotovina, from the Main Staff, and from the commanders who were superior to me. But, since we didn't establish a classical garrison ... tasks that were necessary to the logistics, that's why I was connected to the office of the president. Brian Foster: So, in effect, you were your own authority in Knin, but connected to the office of the president. And that's as far as it goes, is it? Ivan Cermak: Yes, I was connected to the president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that transcript and translations are all -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi, you've seen the interview of General Cermak and he seems to indicate that in fact he wasn't in the line of command of General Cervenko and General Gotovina. Did you see that on the video?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If he wasn't in the line of command of General Cervenko and General Gotovina, can you tell us which line of command, then, he theoretically could have been under?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: On this video footage, I didn't hear at any point General Cermak saying that he was not within the structure of the Split Military District. This wasn't one of the questions put to him at all. Secondly, under the organisational structure of the Croatian Army, within the Split Military District, there is the Knin garrison, and it was pursuant to the decision of President Tudjman that General Cermak was appointed to the commander of that garrison, and that's all. And there is nothing more to state, other than that the Knin garrison was part of the Split Military District. In the footage itself, it is not stated that he was connected to the office of the president. Rather, that he was in communication with the office of president and on occasion in communication with the President Tudjman. In other words, he was not subordinated to President Tudjman. He was not subordinated to General Cervenko either because he is not within the chain of command of garrisons. It is only through Military Districts that he can maintain contact with garrisons. This is the command structure that is in place in the Croatian Army. Now why was the question put to him that he was under one system of authority? This isn't something that was put to him in the footage. He was not within the system of government or connected with the office of the president. This was a question that was apparently put to General Cermak in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You saw at one point in the video that General Cermak says: "I was not a classical garrison commander." Did you note that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What, in the Croatian system, as an expert, can you tell us what a non-classical garrison commander's functions are?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, there is no such thing as a classical or non-classical commander of garrisons. There are commanders of garrisons who can be at the head of larger commands, smaller commands, or independent commands, or commands of some of the Military Districts somewhere. So, it is within the command of the Home Guard battalion in Knin that the commands of the garrison lay. It was never independent. It only had nine persons which were assigned to that irregular non-classical command under the establishment. Furthermore, the Knin garrison did not even have its own logistics base or logistics support to be able to supply the units there. There wasn't something that the minister issued as a decision. Now, as for garrisons, there are no classical or non-classical garrisons. Commands, other hand, are strictly defined as to what particular structure they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
