utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, one suggestion might be that given that a large portion of what was on that video comes from something that is already an exhibit, P2532, and when that was admitted into evidence there was a motion, and my understanding was at the time that Mr. Misetic had the opportunity to put additional portions that he would like added to that translation. I know that it's a partial translation, but perhaps if that could simply be updated with this information rather than having a stand-alone transcript that basically reproduces the same evidence, at least in large part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problem either way, but it was my understanding from our earlier conversation that the Chamber preferred this for sake of convenience to have it marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Carrier would prefer a different thing. I think it's all practicalities rather than anything else. Once chosen this avenue, I think we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once chosen this avenue of saying -- not saying that other avenues would not lead to the same destination, D1675 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could turn to page 3 of this document, which is paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I was unclear, not saying that other avenues would not lead to the same destination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, just by way of background, General Feldi, you may be aware but Mr. Radan worked in -- as the chef de cabinet of President Tudjman during and after Operation Storm. And at paragraph 8, he writes -- or he says in the second sentence: "At some point on 4 August, the president asked us to find Mr. Ivan Cermak, he said he would like to send Mr. Cermak as civilian commander of Knin town immediately after the liberation. As far as I can recall today, I asked the president what a civilian commander meant and he told me that it would be a military person tasked with establishing normal civilian life as soon as possible and collaborating with civilian authorities in that process."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go down to paragraph 10, and it's -- paragraph 10 is on the next page in the Croatian. It says: "The next day, 5 August, we found Mr. Cermak and he immediately came to Tuskanac. I know that finding a formal way of appointing Mr. Cermak as civilian commander of Knin town was a great problem because there was no such position within the establishment structure. When we tried to explain our task with regard to drafting a decree of appointment, we asked the president for guidance and explanation. I understand that the president saw Mr. Cermak primarily as" -- Turn the page. "A businessman and not a soldier in a tradition sense irrespective of the rank he had." And if you go to the last sentence in that paragraph: "As we in collaboration with the military office cannot find legal grounds for appointing Mr. Cermak as civilian manager," and in the Croatian, I believe the phrase is [B/C/S spoken] "we contacted the president's military office asking them to find an appropriate establishment position. The military office drafted and sent for president's signature the decree on the appointment of Cermak as commander of the Knin garrison." Now, that is consistent with what you say in paragraph - let me find it - 3.1.4, which is page 49 of 62 in the English. And in your report there, you wrote that: "Consequently when Colonel General Ivan Cermak arrived in Knin on 6 August, 1995, he did not report to the Split Military District commander at the Knin fortress as new operation commander but, rather, proceeded with the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin with the objectives of providing assistance to the civilian inhabitants and the faster normalization of work and life in the town as well as establishing cooperation and coordination with the UN and EU." Now what I wanted to ask you was: Your report just prior to that section beginning at paragraph 2.3.1, and it's the section marked 2.3, the roles, obligations, and authorities of garrison commanders. And my question to you was that I didn't find anywhere in that section under the HV service regulations anything giving a garrison commander either authority or responsibility to provide assistance to civilian inhabitants, to normalize work and life in a town, and to establish cooperation and coordination with the UN and EU. Could you tell us in your report, in the report 2.3, where a garrison commander under the service regulations has the authority to normalize life in -- with civilian inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: In my report, I started from the position that the rules of service or service regulations of the armed forces was to serve all garrisons in Croatia irrespective of their location and size. Because there were problems in the work of the commands of garrisons in 1992 and 1993, in terms of the implementation of the rules of service, the Chief of the Main Staff ordered that checks be carried out of the functioning of the garrisons in Croatia. Based on the findings of the checks, a new order was drafted, which was called an organisational order for the Chief of Staff and the minister of Defence. I referred to in my report. It was supposed to clarify the role and tasks of the garrisons and their respective commands within the Croatian Army. It was still during the period of time when a large portion of Croatia was under occupation. In the new organisational order, they did not clearly prescribe the rules and -- the tasks and rules that have to be followed by the commanders of garrisons, but in item 1 of the order, it is stated that preparations need to be carried out for the establishment of garrison commands once the occupied areas are liberated. This is precisely what happened in 1995 in Operation Storm in the case of Knin. In the organisational order it was ordered that all garrison commands should have clear specific tasks given the specific circumstances in which those garrisons were. The chief of the Main Staff was duty-bound to prescribe the disposition of all HV units which were supposed to be deployed and billeted in Knin. That was never done. Those units which were in Knin were there in passing, or so to say, they were in operational reserve of the district commander. They were not permanently stationed in the garrison, and according to the rules of service and per the organisational order and instruction they could not be in direct communication with the garrison commander. In the organisational order in the preamble as well as in item 4, concerning the duties of the garrison commanders, such commanders were supposed to establish a system of coordination and cooperation in order to cooperate with the civilian authorities in the area of the garrison. Which type of coordination that was supposed to do was unclear. First and foremost, the priority was to assist the inhabitants. This is precisely what the Knin garrison commander did. I would remind you of the meeting of General Cermak with Mr. Akashi on the 7th in Knin. Immediately after the Akashi-Sarinic agreements had been signed. Akashi met with Cermak and in the two-hour meeting, they set out to clarify the possible tasks that were supposed to be implemented in the Knin garrison area pursuant to the agreement. Cermak undertook that obligation and he used that obligation and the agreement as guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- I think you would agree with me that General Cermak didn't receive his tasks from Mr. Akashi; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who did General Cermak receive his instructions from?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: From no one. General Cermak, during his stay, was visited by many foreign and domestic delegations. He exchanged his views and experience with them, and because of the situation, he was in, he, of his own accord initiated daily coordination meetings with the people in the area. He met, coordinated, and discussed among others with Mr. Pasic, with the chief of the police administration, with the representatives of other utilities such as the head of hospital, the head of the public utility company, so on and so forth. During such meetings he was briefed on the situation. He was trying to push them to do their work. He would tell them, You are here to breathe life into Knin again. And that was his task. He had no HV units of his own in which he would be able to say that he would engage this or that guards units to implement such tasks. This was a different situation. He didn't have such units. He didn't have such authority because he had not given -- he had not been given that authority by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The beginning part of your answer when I said who did General Cermak receive his instructions from, you said: From no one. In the HV how many subordinate officers can begin to do things on their own without having received an instruction or an order from a superior?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, a commander must not sit tight, even without the presence of an order of his own accord or initiative he is supposed to deal with the problems he encountered. If ordered to sent a report by his superior he would do so. Otherwise he would simply tell him, I did this and that. Specifically concerning the Knin situation, please recall the meeting at the fortress when General Cermak reported to the garrison command. He notified them that he arrived to clean up the city and he asked that he be released from the meeting early so that he could go on about his tasks. He only came there to advise them that he was there to assist, to breathe life back into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I feel a little bit like we're going around in a circle, because if a commander doesn't receive an instruction or an order from a superior and decides to take an initiative, he can only take an initiative within the scope of what the rules and regulations of a garrison commander allow him to do. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to section 2.3 in your report, can you tell us which -- the section is titled: The role, obligations, and authorities of garrison commanders. My question to you is: Within section 2.3, can you tell us the provision of the rules or the service regulations which allow a garrison commander to normalize life in -- in a particular -- in his garrison.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I will answer your question directly. The Knin garrison commander was not ordered to go to Knin and to set up a command post there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take this outside the context of the specifics of the Knin garrison. Speaking about garrisons generally, okay? What I'm asking you is, as a general matter, for any garrison, let's say -- let's use the example of the Benkovac garrison. Now, can you tell us in your report in section 2.3, what would have allowed the commander of the Benkovac garrison to normalize life in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: The rules of service of the armed forces states that, at that time, there was peace in Croatia, and that such tasks that Mr. Cermak encountered once he arrived in Knin did not exist. The garrison commander cooperates with the local bodies in terms of regular work and life of the garrison, in terms of order, discipline, conduct of military personnel, as well as organizing different types of events, such as sports competitions and so on and so forth. The problems that existed in Knin were not envisaged by the rules of service. It was not drafted for such conditions, conditions during the period of occupation and immediately afterwards. The taskings of 2.3.1 cannot be compared to the tasks given to the Knin garrison commander once he arrive there after Knin had been liberated. The garrison commander who was for example sitting in Varazdin and Zagreb and Rijeka would go about carrying out his ordinary peacetime tasks, such as due to services, conduct of -- oversight of conduct of military personnel, in public areas, et cetera. Cermak had none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm confused now so I'd like you to clarify something. At page 46, lines 3 and 4, I asked you: Who did General Cermak receive his instructions from; and your answer was: From no one. And now in your last answer, at line -- page 48, lines 15 through 17, you say: "The taskings of 2.3 cannot be compared to the tasks given to the Knin garrison commander once he arrived after Knin had been liberated?" That was the question I had asked you previously: Who gave him the tasks in Knin to -- on what to do after Knin had been liberated?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I will repeat my answer. No one gave him such tasks, not on a daily, weekly, or monthly basis. Once he was sent by the president to Knin on the 5th of August he told him, Go there and help, that ordinary life and work be introduced into the town as soon as possible. That was his principle instruction, and he abided by it in the long run. Another task was go and help the Canadians there and be at their service. You can read that in the presidential transcript of the 7th when he explained why he was sending Cermak to Knin. That was the only instruction that one can find. He did not receive daily instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Please understand this. On the 5th, the operation was still underway. There was still combat. He arrived on the 6th, before the operation was concluded. Therefore, this was no peacetime. One could not sit tight waiting for instructions or wait until the 10th for someone to arrive or -- and give you instructions. General Gotovina, who was his superior, was commanding his units in order to conclude the operation to reach the state border and to prevent any activities on the part of straying enemy soldiers. He had his own tasks. And in terms of the garrison, Cermak was there to organise ordinary life and work there. If you're looking for some daily, weekly or monthly instructions, he received none of that from anyone in particular. He received advice and he received requests from those whom he met daily and coordinated with, from the representatives of the local authorities, civilian police, military police, and various delegations which arrived there, telling him of the problems. He met with the refugees in the camp. They wanted to go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: -- Cermak wanted to have the electricity running as well as other utilities. Those were his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you but you had answered my question. And given your answers, can we -- do I understand you correctly that there is nothing in section 2.3 of your report or anything you can point to in the service regulations generally concerning the authority of a garrison commander to normalise life. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And we're in agreement that in terms of the instructions that he received as to what he was supposed to be doing generally, generally, in Knin, he received directly from the Commander-in-Chief?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: We do not agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: It was only once that he been given a task by the president and that was to go to Knin. That's it. The president told him, Go there and organise -- or organise things for a normal life in the city and go and help the Canadians. That's it. He never received any other instructions from the president. Such evidence does not exist. No document could corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, could you please try to focus your answers to the questions that are put to you by Mr. Misetic. Because Mr. Misetic is already, for a while, trying to get a clear answer first to his question, and I think you have given that, that nothing in the formal rules on the role, obligations, and authorities of the garrison commanders mainly contained in the service regulations of the -- no, the organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline in garrisons, that nothing says that it's a task of a garrison commander to normalise civilian life. Because that's a question he did put to you some ten minutes ago; whereas, it took him ten minutes to get a rather simple answer that was a yes. And do I understand your testimony correctly if you say, Well, whatever these rules tell us, a situation was different, so, therefore, it was done in a way rather different from what the rules tell us, because the only thing that happened was that General Cermak was sent by President Tudjman to Knin to get civilian life being normalised again and to take care of the Canadians, which is relatively far away from the tasks that we find in all the formal regulations, on what the normal task of a garrison commander is. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Feldi, I had read to you a portion from the statement of Mr. Radin. And can you tell us what in Croatian law, rules or regulations is a civilian commander or a civilian manager?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I can freely say that Mr. Radin not a soldier. The phraseology "civilian commander" does not exist in the Croatian Army or in any of its service rules. It was a play of words on his part, if I may say. One cannot appoint a civilian commander because there are no commanders in civilian life. There are commanders in the military and police, but in civilian institutions there are no commanders. One can have managers, or commissioners and so on and forth, but this was just a phrase by Mr. Radin that he used in the context of his statement. Had he known perhaps of the existence of an institution of the command garrison then he may have said, Yes, that he was that, and it was an advice given by the military cabinet, but the tasks and priorities of that garrison commander were to be those issued to him by the president. The term "civilian commander" is misinterpreted as if that person was supposed to go there and command civilians. That is my simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there are no -- or I should -- let me rephrase that. Would you agree with me that neither General Cervenko nor General Gotovina issued orders to General Cermak as to what he should be doing in the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this question? The chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, as well as General Gotovina, did issue orders to General Cermak. But not in the sense you think, in the sense of the things he was supposed to be doing. They simply gave him orders he was supposed to implement. There were such instances in which they issued orders to the garrison commander, although it had probably nothing to do with what you are referring to in terms of civilian assistance. Such orders were not received from General -- by General Cermak from either the chief of the staff or General Gotovina. General Cervenko did send an order on the 21st of August requesting from General Cermak to submit a report on the areas mined, the secret storage of weapons and the possible locations of renegade gangs in the garrison area and so on, and he did receive that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I -- could I -- Mr. Feldi, the interpreters and transcribers have some difficulties in following your speed of speech, so if you would please slow down your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's just one matter on the translation, 53, number 6, we have the word "implement" and a better speaker than me has used the word "receive." 53:6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could seek to verify that. I'll read part of your answer, as it was -- Mr. Feldi, as it was translated and transcribed for us. It reads: "General Cervenko did send an order on the 21st of August requesting from General Cermak to submit a report on the areas mined on illegal storage, the illegal storage of weapons, and the possible locations of the straying enemy soldiers, and he did implement that order." Is that a correct translation and transcript of the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was not illegal storages of weapons. Rather, secret caches of arms left behind by members of the RSK army and could possibly be used by stragglers of that army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to verify the accuracy of the transcript. I'm not seeking any further exploring the matter. So you say illegal should be understood as secret storage of weapons. Any other matter which is not correctly or accurately transcribed or translated for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is that -- was this the matter you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was another matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- but you we can look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I do not know exactly what the matter is because I do not -- I'm not a position to personally verify the matter. You can deal with it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D818 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On this issue, General Feldi - I'll wait for the English translation to come up - it's a request from General Gotovina to General Cermak. Would you agree with me that it's not typical that a Military District Commander requests anything of a garrison commander, but, rather, orders him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I will use a soldier's saying to answer. Authority, even when requesting, in fact orders. So whenever a subordinate receives a request from a superior, he needs to implement it. The commander can issue an order or a request. In other words, he can say either, Do this and that, or, Please do this and that. At any rate, this is something that a superior would do to the subordinate. What we have here is a case from September, where the chief of the communications department, Mr. Lukovic, acted on his own initiative and went to Bosnia-Herzegovina via Strmica without General Cermak's approval or knowledge. He had on him a pass that had been signed by General Cermak. This is something that Mr. Lukovic himself admitted when he said that he made a mistake. He was supposed to escort a French delegation via Sinj rather than via Strmica. So this a specific example where the commander demands something from a subordinate. An order is an of an operational nature. Every request has inherently an imperative in it. This is something that the subordinate needs to act upon and carry out because there is what the commander seeks. I spoke to Lukovic directly on this particular issue described in the document here and this was confirmed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Again, my question is of a general nature. As a matter of practice in the HV, superior commanders don't request anything of their subordinates, do they? They order them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: We could state that this is indeed so, when it comes to the procedure of implementing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be a circular reasoning. If it's not an order, then he doesn't have to implement it. Let me ask it a different way. Commanders in Military Districts issue orders to their subordinate garrison commanders --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- in the HV?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many requests from General Gotovina did you see in preparing for this report to the garrison commander in Sinj, in Zadar, in Split, in Benkovac? How many times did he not order the garrison commander, instead he issued a request? How many such orders did you find?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Not a single one, save for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to section 1.5.50 of your report, which is paragraph -- I'm sorry, page 38 of 48 -- sorry. I'm looking at Part 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's page 38 of 62. And page 34 of 57 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is your section -- this is the conclusion part of this section. And in the English if we could turn the page. And in the Croatian, if could you look at bullet point 5 of your report in the Croatian. And it's the first bullet point of 39 of 62 in the English. You write: "Reporting," and it's in bold, "as a component of principle of command and control is established as a permanent obligation of the subordinated person within the subordination system and it is regulated by the service regulations of the armed forces, the rules governing the structure and operation," now this relates to the military police, "and in all orders which are issued by the superiors of the military police." Now, you agree with me that reporting is also a component or principle of command and control within the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that within the military line, a subordinated person has a permanent obligation to report to a superior on what he or she is doing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Can you clarify the term "permanent"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just reading what you wrote in your report here. What did you mean when you wrote: "Reporting as a component or principle of command and control is established as a permanent obligation of the subordinated person ..." What did you mean by "permanent obligation"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Permanent obligation, yes, but not at all times and on every -- and every day. The reporting is part of the obligations within the superior/subordinate relationship. It is one of the obligations that the subordinated person has in relation to the superior. The superior, in turn, has to define precisely in what manner, at what time, and through which system the subordinates are to report to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we spend another five minutes on what the word "permanent" means, I do understand that by using the word "permanent," you did not refer to incidental reporting but that it was an ongoing obligation to keep the superior updated throughout reports. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus on the main issue touched upon in the question, rather than to see all side roads to see what's -- if we would turn to the left, what we would finally find there, or turn to the right, what we finally find there. I'd rather see where we end up if we continue on the main road as indicated by the question. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many reports -- how many reports did General Cermak send to General Gotovina in your review of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I can state at this time that he sent between five and six of them. There may have been more that I did not take into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which reports are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: The first one is the report on the head count of the command of the Knin garrison, was sent to the commander of the Military District between -- or, rather, at the end of August and at the end of September. So there were two of them. So in August, there were ten persons, and in September, there were four persons in the commands, according to the establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, again, Mr. Misetic is not interested to hear what exactly was said in those reports but what subjects were covered by those reports. So you tell us the head count of the command, two reports. Whatever the numbers were. Other subjects, please, of reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. One of the reports was sent to the Chief of the Main Staff on the 25th of August, and the same was copied to the commander of the Military District, as he was obliged to do under his superior/subordinate relationship. Then there was the report on the write-off of housing units in Knin, and -- the abandoned housing units in Knin, where he reported that Knin did not have a single such dwelling at its disposal. These were official documents, official reports. I am not aware of any other. What sort of communication they had on a daily basis, if they exchanged information, that is something I have no information on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, you earlier said five or six. You have now mentioned two on counting the heads, and two others, one of them not directly sent to Mr. Gotovina but copied to him. That makes four. Any others, that would bring us to five or six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember at this time, Your Honour. If I do, I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to paragraph 3.1.4 of your report, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is page 49 of 62 in the English. And page 45 of 57 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is again that paragraph where -- I'm going to read the second part of that paragraph where you wrote: "But rather" -- and you're talking about General Cermak. "But rather proceeded with the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin with the objectives of providing assistance to the civilian inhabitants and the faster normalisation of work and life in the town, as well as establishing co-operation and coordination with the UN and EU." Now, with respect to the first task, other than the documents you have already identified, are there any reports from General Cermak to General Gotovina about the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I've already said that the command of the Knin garrison had not received an order to relocate from Sibenik to Knin, nor did such an order ask of the Knin garrison to send a report to the Split Military District. I did not find any documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tell me on what authority, then -- on what authority could General Cermak have decided on his own to move the Knin garrison from Sibenik to Split? I mean, a garrison commander on his own cannot decide he's moving the garrison to a different location, can he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, was there a slip of the tongue where you said to move --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Knin garrison from Sibenik to Split when you meant to say from Sibenik to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on whose authority was that move made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the decision by the president does not state that he was duty-bound to establish the Knin garrison. Rather, that he was assigned to the post of the commander of the Knin garrison. So he immediately set off for Knin to establish the garrison there. The news about General Cermak's appointment to the position of the commander of the Knin garrison was immediately broadcast. I, myself, heard it over the radio at midnight. Everyone who was in contact at the time knew that the former commander of the Knin garrison, Marko Vojevic [as interpreted], was appointed the deputy commander of the Knin garrison. In other words, Gojevic, who had formally hitherto been commander of the Knin garrison, had to go and meet up with Cermak in Knin. And I don't have any information that Gojevic had been given an order that he should go to Knin and set up a garrison there. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi, I'm just reading your report here, and in paragraph 3.1.4, you say that General Cermak proceeded with the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin. On whose orders did he proceed with the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Please bear in mind the fact that the document as such does not exist. What is in existence is the video footage of General Cermak reporting to the command -- commander of the Military District at the fortress in Knin on the 6th of August, that he informed him that he was going take charge of normalising the situation in Knin. This is what we have in the footage. We have statements, furthermore, showing that the Knin garrison was being established, and his assistant for logistics accompanied General Cermak on his way to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, again, you are explaining us what evidence there is that the Knin garrison was established. The question, however, was a different one. The question was: Under whose authority did, as you write in your report, Mr. Cermak proceed with the establishment of the garrison commands. I think there is not that much doubt that it was done. But on whose authority? That was the question that Mr. Misetic put to you. Could you tell us who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the duties of the commander of a garrison are strictly prescribed. When he arrived in Knin, he reported to the commander of the Military District to whom he is subordinated, and the powers to command over the garrison are conferred upon him by his superior. When he arrived in Knin he went to the commander of the Military District, and then he was supposed to assume his duties as the garrison commander. That's all that had to do with his powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going stop you again. We earlier established that whatever the regulations say about what the tasks were of a garrison commander, that that would not apply. That is my first observation. My second observation is that you are telling us whom Mr. Cermak addressed once he had arrived Knin; whereas, the question was a different one. Under whose authority he proceeded to establish the garrison command in the -- Knin. I got the impression from your report, but please correct me when I misunderstood your report, I understood that he was sent there under the authority of the president of the Republic, the Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Tudjman. Is that the authority who would have allowed him or instructed him to establish the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's correct, Your Honour. By appointing him a -- Knin garrison commander, President Tudjman granted him all the powers to do his job. He tasked him with restoring normalcy to Knin as soon as possible, and with cooperating with UN personnel in the area. These were the tasks directly given to him by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you give us all kind of details you were not asked for. We were just seeking who was the authority which allowed Mr. Cermak to establish the Knin garrison or, as you said, proceeded to establish the Knin garrison. From what I now, again, understand, what you're saying - but, again, correct me when I'm wrong - you're saying by appointing Mr. Cermak as the Knin garrison commander, whatever tasks be given to him, that is implied that, since there was no -- not yet a Knin garrison command, that it was implied that that is what had to be established by the newly appointed commander. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know how much time you'd still need. I can imagine that takes a bit more time than you anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes. Then I think that it, nevertheless, would be wise to have the break now. We have a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi, we left off, the Presiding Judge had asked you a question and you agreed with him that it would have been implied to General Cermak that since there was not yet a Knin garrison command, it was implied that that is what had to be established by the newly appointed commander. And you answered" -- he asked you, is that correctly understood? And you said: "Yes, Your Honour." Now going back to paragraph 3.1.4 of your report, in establishing the Knin garrison command in the town of Knin, who did General Cermak sent his reports about the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would like to be more precise in my answer. The command post of the garrison in Knin was set up by virtue of the decision on the establishment of garrison commands from 1993. This specifically was the establishment of the garrison command in the town of Knin. As a command post it had existed prior to that date in a different location. But once General Cermak assumed his role, he was supposed to establish the command post by virtue of the president's decision in the town of Knin. This was not to be a new command post. It had been in existence in the years preceding that, and the then garrison commander, Brigadier Bojovic was reporting, and once General Cermak arrived there, he reported - that is to say, the brigadier reported - to General Cermak as his new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All of that is understood. All I'm asking you is: When he established the command post in the town of Knin, who did he report that fact to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, in 3.1.4, I state that General Cermak initiated the establishing of the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I'm going to stop you. Did General Cermak establish the garrison command in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he report to anyone, and, if so, to whom, that he had done so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A separate report on the setting up of the Knin garrison command, which would be headed by General Cermak, was not sent to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Could we try -- could we try to keep matters as focussed and as -- and as simple as possible. If Mr. Misetic would like to know further details such as the -- the date of reporting, or how -- to other -- to whom else a report was addressed, he will certainly ask you about it, so try to focus on the question that was put to you, and it was quite simple. Mr. Cermak did establish and no separate report and that was sent to anyone. It's just two lines that would provide Mr. Misetic with the information he was seeking. If you want to seek any further information, please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Continuing on in paragraph 3.1.4 you say that he established the command, garrison command in the town of Knin with the objectives of providing assistance to the civilian inhabitants. Now did you find any report from General Cermak to General Gotovina reporting on his work in providing assistance to the civilian inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it continues on: He was also working on, "the faster normalization of work and life in the town?" Did you find any report from General Cermak to General Gotovina reporting about what he was doing in terms of faster normalization of work and life in the town?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I did. Your Honour, it is also an answer I still owe to you about the number of reports that Cermak sent to the Military District in Split. There was a report on his attempts to locate the vehicles and engineering equipment which went missing in the area of the garrison. He requested assistance to locate such vehicles and to establish order in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I guess I had put that in the last category of your report, and I was going to get to that, which is the task of establishing cooperation and coordination with the UN and EU. But in terms of as I understand what faster normalization of work and live in the town, it means establishing electricity in the town, the water-supply, soup kitchens, et cetera. Are there any reports from General Cermak to General Gotovina about how he was progressing on the faster normalization of work and life in the town, including things like reopening businesses, et cetera, in the area?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there is no such a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then in the last objective of General Cermak in your paragraph 3.1.4 is establishing cooperation and coordination with the UN and the EU. In addition to the report that you now referred to as -- asking for assistance in locating missing UN vehicle, did you find any other reports from General Cermak to General Gotovina, for example, if General Cermak had a meeting with members of UNCIVPOL or UNCRO or UNMO, did he report on those meetings to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: He did not report him on such matters and he was not duty-bound to. He sent his meeting reports to the UN office, which existed in Knin next to the Military District of Split command post there. That office was not under Cermak and did not fall within the command post of the military -- of the garrison in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, General Feldi, you had earlier agreed with me that a subordinate has a permanent obligation to inform or report to -- to report to his superior. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes, that is prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that would include, if a garrison commander felt he was a subordinate of the Military District Commander, if he had a meeting with the UN where various issues are raised concerning potentially the Croatian Army, he has a separate obligation to report to his superior; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: If that is specifically prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't qualify your answer when I asked you before about whether a subordinate in the Croatian Army, in the military, has a permanent obligation to report to his superior. You agreed with me without qualification. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I did, and it is so prescribed. A subordinate is duty-bound to send reports to his superior about the tasks he had received from the superior. That is coordination. If he had not received a task, there is no report to be sent about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if General Gotovina was not the one who tasked General Cermak with coordinating with the UN and the EU, then you're saying he wouldn't have had an obligation to send any reports back to General Cermak about his communications with the UN and EU -- sorry. He wouldn't have had an obligation to send any reports back to General Gotovina about his meetings with the UN and the EU. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: It needs to be understood that keeping contact with the UN did not fall under the authority of the garrison commander. Rather, it was, under the authority of the UN liaison office which was the only office responsible to do so and to send reports on that topic. General Cermak, as the garrison commander, was duty-bound, and please go to D0034, which is the organisational order --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: -- in which, in item 3, the garrison commander, is duty-bound to establish cooperation and coordination with other bodies and institutions of the Ministry of Defence, per tasks under their authority. Pursuant to that, he established cooperation and coordination with the UN office through which he established all contacts with representatives of the UN, the EU, and UNPROFOR; that is to say, UNCRO. He did not send reports on that topic to the Military District Commander because the Military District Commander received such reports directly from the office referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 68, line 13, it should be subordination, not coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi, you're saying that General Cermak had an obligation under the regulations to have contacts with the UN and the EU; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: No, it is not. There is not such a provision in the regulations. He needs to coordinate and cooperate with the office of the Ministry of Defence responsible for liaising with the UN and the EU, not the garrison commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But he was coordinating directly with international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification. You said: "He needs to coordinate and cooperate with the office of the Ministry of Defence responsible for liaising with the UN and the EU, and then the last portion of your answer was: "Not the garrison commands." Which comes as a bit of a surprise, because the questions were focussing on reporting to the Military District, rather than to the garrison command, which is the same as the reporting entity. Is that what you intended to say, Mr. Feldi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you intended to say that he was -- he had to coordinate and cooperate with the office of the Ministry of the Defence and not with the Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not with the UN. The issue was cooperation with the UN, not with the Military Districts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the contacts with the UN and the EU are not found anywhere in the regulations and where a specific part of the -- apparently of the appointment by President Tudjman. Now you referred, in relation to a question about reporting, you related to section 3 of D34 which reads that the -- the garrison commands are required to establish cooperation and coordination of tasks of the garrison with administrations and departments for defence, departments for care, stationary telecommunications and information systems, departments of the MORH headquarters, administrations and other bodies, and institutions of the MORH, MUP ministry and other government administration organs. Now, I understood your reference to this paragraph that there was an obligation to coordinate and cooperate with many but not with the operational military command. Is that your explanation for the line of reporting on the relations with the UN and the EU; that is, that that would go to the Ministry of Defence but not to the operational commands of the armed forces in the Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm under the impression that we are speaking at cross purposes. I did not mention any cooperation on the part of the military garrison commander with the Military District Commanders, and did I not speak of coordination in those terms. Secondly, I said, and I repeat, that the garrison commander was duty-bound to establish cooperation and coordination with the bodies of the Ministry of Defence and the UN -- office for UN is a MOD office with its seat in Knin. General Cermak, as the garrison commander, did -- was not duty-bound to directly communicate with the UN and the European community. This could be done only through that office, which was the only body authorised to communicate and cooperate. That is to say, liaison between HV commanders and representatives of the UN, the EU, and so on and so forth. This is prescribed by the existing regulations. If I may, Your Honour, General Cermak could not speak English and was unable to directly communicate with any officers and employees of the UN. He never even tried to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I don't speak any B/C/S. Nevertheless, I consider our communication of a rather direct nature. You explained to us that he was not -- he was not -- not to directly communicate with the UN. But did he communicate with the UN and not through the intermediary of the office you just mentioned? I mean, what should be and what was -- was there direct communication between General Cermak and the UN or the EU?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not come across such an example in any document or report. Whenever General Cermak had a meeting, there was also either the head of the office for the UN or concern liaison officers from the office who also acted as interpreters and those who established contact. There is evidence of that because the UN liaison officers turned to the office for the UN to cooperate or arrange a meeting with General Cermak. The other way around was the same thing. If General Cermak wanted a meeting with UN representatives, then he used that office to put through a request to meet up. That was the practice. At least to the extent I was ascertained through my research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Correspondence, would that go through that office as well, or would it be direct correspondence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no direct written communication. It all went through the office. They received mail, translated it, and acquainted General Cermak with it. They also received General Cermak's response, translated it, and then sent it via liaison officers to General Forand or others. Numerous reports testify to that. Those reports were sent by the UN office in Knin through their duty service or by Mr. Lukovic personally to Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness trailed off. We did not hear the last person's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said: "Those reports were sent by the UN office in Knin through their duty service or by Mr. Lukovic personally to Zagreb." And then you added something. Could you repeat what you then added?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I concluded my sentence by saying that the office for the UN prepared -- sorry, received letters from the UN or the European community, translated them, and handed them over to General Cermak. If General Cermak wanted to establish contact or to respond, he would provide a text to Lukovic or his liaison officers in the office for the UN in Knin, which, in turn, would have that translated and forwarded. If General Cermak wanted to meet any foreign representatives he used the office to arrange for a meeting. If any UN representatives be it General Forand or any -- anyone other wanted to meet with General Cermak, they used the office and its liaison officers to convey that information to Cermak. That was the procedure in terms of cooperation and coordination with that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The way in which you describe it gives me the impression that it was secretarial services rather than involvement in the substance of the communication. Is that impression correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially, Your Honour. There were contacts that the office for the UN maintained with the EU or the UN in Knin without General Cermak's knowledge. They're responsible for cooperating with the UN for the entire Sector South for that whole area of Croatia. If it had to do with certain other tasks or meetings, such things were done without General Cermak's knowledge. He didn't need to know about that, and he did not participate in such activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was the query over the name that mentioned, and the interpreter -- and it's a name familiar to the Court. It was Plestina, p-l-e-s-t-i-n-a, and if anyone wants to, they can check that, page 72, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although where the witness said he had finished his answer that you -- you're giving some additional evidence, but it can be checked on the audio by anyone who has any concerns about the accuracy at this moment, Mr. Kay, I don't think that the Chamber has any concerns. But everyone who would like to check can do so. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Feldi, in one of your prior answers to me you said -- I'll just check that. It's page 68, lines 14 to 16: "A subordinate is duty-bound to send reports to his superior about the tasks he had received from the superior." And I believe you and I are in agreement that these tasks about normalization of life, he received directly from President Tudjman and not from General Cervenko or General Gotovina. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We had been talking -- you answered that this duty of a subordinate to report exists, and therefore, if President Tudjman was the one who gave him the instruction, and at page -- you indicated at page 50, beginning at line 19, that the president told him, Go there and organise or organise things for a normal life in the city and go and help the Canadians." Now, if the Commander-in-Chief gave him an instruction to do that, and if a duty exists for a subordinate to report and he wasn't reporting on those topics to General Gotovina or General Cervenko, you would expect that those reports would go back to the Commander-in-Chief. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: I don't know if one would expect that, but did I not come across a single report that was sent to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as an expert. Your testimony was, again, page 68, line 14: "A subordinate is duty-bound do send reports to his superior about the tasks he had received from the superior." So, I'm going to ask my question again. You would expect that General Cermak would have sent his reports directly to the commander who had issued him those tasks, which, in this case was the Commander-in-Chief. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: The Commander-in-Chief said so on the transcript. As to what General Cermak and the president discussed when they met in Tuskanac not even Mr. Radin knows that and nor do I. There is no transcript of that meeting. I cannot claim that he was duty-bound to report to the president, because we don't know whether the president told him, Go there and report regularly about the situation. If he had told him that then it would have been expected from Cermak to send reports to him, but I did not find any piece of information to that extent, to the president ordering him to do so. I did not come across a single report he personally sent to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, again, this is the transcript at page 50 beginning at line 18, your testimony was: "It was only once that he been given a task by the president. That was to go to Knin. That's it. The president told him, Go there and organise or organise things for a normal life in the city and go and help the Canadians. That's it. He never received any other instructions from the president." Now, what was your basis for saying that the president had told him to organise things for a normal life in the city and go help the Canadians?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: The transcripts of the meeting at the president's office on the 7th of August, 1995, when Mr. Radic [as interpreted] and other participants in the meeting, complained, among other things of problems with the UN. Then the president said that he had sent General Cermak to Knin, an excellent businessman, an honest man, who would help restore normal life there quickly and who would help the Canadians. He told Zuzul to convey that information to the Canadians who were interested in the situation in Sector South based on the information they received from General Forand. This is something that you can find in the transcript of that meeting. That particular exchange between the president and Zuzul. Reading the transcript I concluded that the president had dispatched them over there with these two basic tasks, i.e., to help restore normal life and work in the town as soon as possible and to be at the disposal and of service to the Canadians. However, the transcript does not state that he was duty-bound to help the UN, that he was duty-bound to help all the international forces and the UN. This isn't what the transcript says. The transcript says that he should help the Canadians. Therefore, it follows from the transcript that he had used the office for the UN to establish cooperation with General Forand and other representatives of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now that we have established that you concluded that he was sent there with two basic tasks: One to help restore normal life and work in the town as soon as possible; and, two, to be at disposal and of service to the Canadians. My question, again, is: Based on your understanding and what you have written here about the duties of a subordinate to report to his superior and your testimony earlier, that he has a duty to report to a superior who actually issued him the tasks, would you have expected, then, that General Cermak, as the superior, would have reported on these two tasks that you have identified to the Commander-in-Chief?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI
utterances.text: As a soldier and a general, I would have expected as much. However, let me remind you that on the 26th of August when the president arrived in Knin, General Cermak reported to him on the activities that were undertaken and the tasks he was occupied with. This was a personal report to the president who had dispatched him to Knin. You can see that from the documentation reflecting Mr. Cermak's address to the president upon the arrival of the freedom train in Knin. He was their Commander-in-Chief, in command of an army. And he sent him to Knin and told him, I will ask you -- call you to account to see what you have done. There were reports that the president received as well through various channels on steps taken to restore normalcy in Knin and the steps taken to establish cooperation with the UN, and you heard about it from the statement Mr. Cermak gave in the interview in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to you, Mr. Carrier, to cross-examine the witness, I would have one question. I think you mentioned Mr. Lukovic twice and you said that you spoke with him about a certain subject and that he had confirmed your interpretation of the events. Now, in your methodology, I see no interviews. Could you tell me, did you have an interview with Mr. Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I -- I had spoken to Mr. Lukovic on several occasions, and it had to do with the overall activities of the office for the UN of the Ministry of Defence and the UN department in Knin during and after Operation Storm. I know Mr. Lukovic and used to come across him out in the field when touring the theatre of war, and I was familiar with his work and his duties. Lukovic made a mistake when he set off for Strmica. This is what prompted General Cervenko to write a letter to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, you're, again, on quite a lot of side roads, where I just asked you whether you did have an interview; that is, a meeting specifically scheduled to obtain information in a conversation from Mr. Lukovic. Did you have such an interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you see him for the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly three years ago. By your leave, the information concerning Lukovic's trip towards Strmica was something that I found in the document that he had sent to Plestina and for which he had been reprimanded by Cermak. I didn't speak to him about it. I don't know how such a conclusion could have been drawn that I had discussed this matter with Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I made a mistake. I mixed up Lukavic and Lukovic apparently. You said -- and we were then talking about ... you said at a certain moment, I spoke to Lukovic directly on this issue in the document here, and we were then looking at D818, and it was about requesting or ordering something. And then you said: "I spoke to Lukovic" -- and perhaps that's the same as Lukavic, I do not know, "directly on the issue in the document here and this was confirmed to me." Now I wondered at what occasion you did speak to Lukovic directly on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise if the interpreters made mistake. I told you that I last contacted Lukovic some three years ago. As for this specific case I found the information in the document that Lukovic signed and sent to Plestina. He said that he had taken the French via Strmica and that he had been reprimanded or cautioned for this fact by Cermak. I did not, however, include the document in my report. I can refer to it, and I can include it in the general documentation in support of my report. This was why General Gotovina requested that Cermak no longer allowed such individuals to go across the area under the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in relation to what a subordinate is expected to do - that means request, or order, whatever - you said, "This is something that the subordinate needs to act upon" -- apparently referring to the request by Mr. Gotovina not to escort international observers in certain areas -- "something that the subordinate needs to act upon and carry out because that is what the commander seeks." And then you said: "I spoke to Lukovic directly on this issue in the document here, and there was confirmed to me." My simple question was: When did you discuss this with Lukovic and at what occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two to three years ago, when I was working on the material concerning Operation Storm. I spoke to Lukovic and Plestina in the archives on the Ministry of Defence, approximately three years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it in any context of preparing the report which is now before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not. I didn't know that I was going to write the report at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Carrier, perhaps it might not be a good idea to start for just a couple of minutes the cross-examination for the Prosecution unless there's a matter which you consider appropriate to deal with in five minutes and then continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think I can get much done in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you give us any indication, also in view of the way in which cross-examination develops, how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I had estimated four sessions. I know that Mr. Misetic had estimated about 30 to 45 minutes and took significantly longer, and I'm anticipating it could take me somewhat longer. I will do my best to try to finish in four sessions or maybe even in three, if I can perhaps revisit some of the issues tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That may be of some guidance for the Cermak Defence as well as to when to have the next witness to be stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Arrangements have already been put in train for the next witness and he will be here on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which most likely will not be tomorrow in view of the time claimed by the Prosecution. Certainly more than -- three sessions or more, which means that the witness doesn't have to be stand by tomorrow, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Flights are booked, Your Honour, arrangements made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The only thing I'm saying is, instead of someone who expects that he is required to be in the courtroom tomorrow, instead of waiting here for five hours to find out that there's no time to even start his examination-in-chief, that I take it that the witness will know at its earliest the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour can take it that we will deal with all the witnesses so that they are here when necessary and are not kept necessarily waiting. We will be dealing with it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you do not mind that the Chamber, of course, has also its own concerns and responsibility for witnesses. It's not in any way to suggest that you would not be precise in that respect, Mr. Kay. Mr. Feldi, we'd like to see you back tomorrow, the 23rd of September, 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. And I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is testimony that you have given already today, or whether that is testimony still to be given in the day or the days to come. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Feldi out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask that -- whether I'm allowed to take my expert report and the notes I made along, whereas all the supporting documentation is something I'd like to leave here. If you agree -- I don't know what the practice of the Tribunal is -- or should I leave everything behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't see why not. It's his report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I have no issue with him taking it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you take your report and your personal notes with you. Please, especially for the personal notes, take them with you tomorrow. Yes? Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would just like to put on the record a practical matter. On the 19th of August the Prosecution has filed a request for clarification. That is, a clarification in relation to the deadlines for responding to the submission of expert reports, specifically in relation to Mr. Feldi. That report was not presented in one piece but at -- in a sequence of moments. I think the Chamber gave informally that clarification. That is, that we would start counting -- I think it was on the 17th of August, when, in a submission by the Cermak Defence, Part 3 of the report was filed. First, since there is a filed request for clarification, it's appropriate to put on the record that the clarification has, although informally been given by the Chamber in accordance with what I just said, and I wonder in view of what happened after that, whether there's any further need to address this matter, or whether the matter has been dealt with in its entirety. Because we have then a consolidated report and we had some corrections to the report. But that, I take it, would not trigger any further time-limits for the Prosecution to -- to make up its mind as to the -- whether or not to accept the report and whether they want to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We just understood it to just be filing what we did, so ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this being on the record, we adjourn until tomorrow morning, 22nd of September -- 23rd of September - I stand corrected - 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
